ten_second.headline: Supported a certification condition for the earlier fentanyl bill
ten_second.practical_choice: Whether H.R. 27 should take effect only after HHS and DOJ jointly certified that it would reduce overdose deaths.
ten_second.member_action_and_result: Foushee voted Yea. The amendment failed 182-226.

thirty_second.prior_baseline: H.R. 27 would otherwise take effect without this certification step.
thirty_second.mechanism: The amendment would condition the bill's changes on a joint HHS-DOJ Federal Register certification.
thirty_second.affected: Federal agencies implementing the scheduling and enforcement changes, researchers, and people affected by the controlled-substance rules.
thirty_second.scale_or_timing: The condition would apply before the bill's changes took effect.
thirty_second.what_happened_next: The amendment failed; the House then passed H.R. 27 without it.

two_minute.detail: This was a substantive condition on implementation, not a generic procedural vote.

supporter_argument.argument: She argued that the certification was an evidence guardrail tied to overdose reduction.

two_minute.argument_boundary: These are attributed floor arguments and do not establish why Foushee voted Yea.
two_minute.later_history: A related Senate bill, S. 331, later passed the House and became law.
caveats: This action and the later bill votes are one policy episode.
The vote does not establish motive.

ten_second.headline: Opposed the House's earlier permanent fentanyl-scheduling bill
ten_second.practical_choice: Whether to pass H.R. 27 after the certification amendment failed.
ten_second.member_action_and_result: Foushee voted Nay. The House passed the bill 312-108.

thirty_second.prior_baseline: Temporary classwide scheduling for fentanyl-related substances was already in place.
thirty_second.mechanism: The bill would make classwide Schedule I treatment permanent and set related penalty and research-registration rules.
thirty_second.affected: Federal enforcement and research agencies, researchers, defendants, and communities affected by fentanyl-related substances.
thirty_second.scale_or_timing: This was the House's February version, not the later enacted bill.
thirty_second.what_happened_next: H.R. 27 passed the House but did not itself become law.

two_minute.detail: The vote followed rejection of a proposed overdose-reduction certification condition.

supporter_argument.argument: Supporters argued that permanent classwide scheduling would strengthen enforcement while preserving a research pathway.

two_minute.argument_boundary: The arguments describe the bill-level dispute; they do not identify Foushee's reason for voting Nay.
two_minute.later_history: The Senate later sent the House the related S. 331, which became Public Law 119-26.
caveats: H.R. 27 and S. 331 are related but not identical actions.
A Nay does not assign a reason.

ten_second.headline: Supported the later fentanyl bill that became law
ten_second.practical_choice: Whether to pass the Senate bill making classwide fentanyl-related-substance scheduling permanent with research provisions.
ten_second.member_action_and_result: Foushee voted Yea. The bill passed 321-104 and later became law.

thirty_second.prior_baseline: Temporary classwide scheduling remained in place while Congress considered a permanent framework.
thirty_second.mechanism: S. 331 made classwide Schedule I treatment permanent and included registration and rulemaking provisions for research.
thirty_second.affected: Federal enforcement and research agencies, researchers, defendants, and communities affected by fentanyl-related substances.
thirty_second.scale_or_timing: The President signed Public Law 119-26 on July 16, 2025.
thirty_second.what_happened_next: The measure became law after this House vote.

two_minute.detail: The enacted law combined permanent scheduling with provisions concerning research registration and agency rulemaking.

supporter_argument.argument: Supporters argued that permanent classwide scheduling would strengthen enforcement while preserving a research pathway.

two_minute.argument_boundary: The debate supplies competing policy arguments; it does not explain Foushee's change across related measures.
caveats: The earlier H.R. 27 vote and this vote belong to one episode.
The votes do not reveal why her position differed.

ten_second.headline: Opposed a program for eligible officers to buy retired service firearms
ten_second.practical_choice: Whether to require a federal program allowing eligible current and retired officers to buy certain retired agency-issued firearms.
ten_second.member_action_and_result: Foushee voted Nay. The House passed the bill 234-182.

thirty_second.prior_baseline: No government-wide statutory purchase program with these terms was in place.
thirty_second.mechanism: GSA would establish a program for eligible officers in good standing to buy qualifying retired firearms at salvage value during a six-month window.
thirty_second.affected: Participating federal agencies and eligible current or retired law-enforcement officers.
thirty_second.scale_or_timing: GSA would establish the program within one year; specified weapons would remain excluded.
thirty_second.what_happened_next: The bill went to the Senate and was not enacted as of review.

two_minute.detail: Eligibility, transfer rules, exclusions, and agency participation were defined in the House-passed text.

supporter_argument.argument: Supporters argued that officers could retain familiar service weapons while agencies avoided disposal costs.

two_minute.argument_boundary: These attributed arguments do not establish which concern, if any, explains Foushee's Nay.
two_minute.later_history: Received in the Senate after House passage.
caveats: The bill covered eligible officers and qualifying firearms, not every officer or weapon.
House passage did not create the program.

ten_second.headline: Supported federal reporting on attacks and officer wellness
ten_second.practical_choice: Whether to require DOJ reports on attacks against law-enforcement officers, reporting-system feasibility, and mental-health and wellness resources.
ten_second.member_action_and_result: Foushee voted Yea. The House passed the bill 403-11.

thirty_second.prior_baseline: Federal data and reporting on these subjects were spread across existing systems and programs.
thirty_second.mechanism: DOJ would prepare reports on attacks, reporting feasibility, and officer mental-health and wellness resources.
thirty_second.affected: Law-enforcement agencies and officers, DOJ, and policymakers using the resulting reports.
thirty_second.scale_or_timing: The bill set 270-day deadlines for the principal reports.
thirty_second.what_happened_next: The bill went to the Senate and was not enacted as of review.

two_minute.detail: The House action authorized information gathering and reporting; it did not itself create a new criminal penalty.

supporter_argument.argument: Supporters argued that better data could guide officer-safety and wellness policy.

two_minute.argument_boundary: No adequate stage-specific opposing argument was found in the reviewed official materials; none is inferred from the 11 Nays.
two_minute.later_history: Received in the Senate after House passage.
caveats: The reviewed official materials did not provide a fair stage-specific opposing case.
A Yea does not establish a position on policies Congress might later consider using the reports.

ten_second.headline: Opposed replacing D.C.'s police-pursuit restrictions
ten_second.practical_choice: Whether Congress should replace D.C.'s pursuit restrictions with a broader pursuit requirement and specified risk and effectiveness exceptions.
ten_second.member_action_and_result: Foushee voted Nay. The House passed the bill 245-182.

thirty_second.prior_baseline: D.C. law restricted when Metropolitan Police Department officers could initiate vehicle pursuits.
thirty_second.mechanism: The substitute would require pursuit in specified felony and violent-misdemeanor circumstances when other apprehension means were unavailable, subject to exceptions, and require a DOJ technology report.
thirty_second.affected: D.C. residents, drivers, police officers, local officials, and DOJ.
thirty_second.scale_or_timing: The measure would alter local pursuit rules and require a federal report.
thirty_second.what_happened_next: The bill went to the Senate and was not enacted as of review.

two_minute.detail: The vote was on the Rules Committee substitute, whose exceptions matter to describing the policy accurately.

supporter_argument.argument: Supporters argued that broader pursuit authority would help police apprehend people suspected of serious offenses.

two_minute.argument_boundary: The debate presents institutional and safety arguments; it does not establish Foushee's reason for voting Nay.
two_minute.later_history: Received in the Senate after House passage.
caveats: The substitute included exceptions; it was not an unconditional pursuit mandate.
A Nay does not reveal which objection drove the vote.

ten_second.headline: Opposed repealing most of D.C.'s 2022 policing reform law
ten_second.practical_choice: Whether Congress should repeal most provisions of D.C.'s 2022 policing reform law and restore prior rules, subject to exceptions in the substitute.
ten_second.member_action_and_result: Foushee voted Nay. The House passed the bill 233-190.

thirty_second.prior_baseline: D.C.'s 2022 law governed police practices, disclosure, discipline, and oversight.
thirty_second.mechanism: The committee substitute would repeal most of that law and restore prior provisions while retaining specified exceptions.
thirty_second.affected: D.C. residents, police officers, oversight bodies, courts, and local government.
thirty_second.scale_or_timing: The measure addressed neck restraints, body-camera access, disciplinary records, and other policing rules.
thirty_second.what_happened_next: The bill went to the Senate and was not enacted as of review.

two_minute.detail: The exact committee substitute matters: describing it as repeal of the entire law would overstate its reach.

supporter_argument.argument: Supporters argued that undoing the D.C. law's restrictions would improve recruitment, retention, and public safety.

two_minute.argument_boundary: These are attributed arguments about the substitute and do not establish Foushee's motive.
two_minute.later_history: Received in the Senate after House passage.
caveats: The substitute repealed most, not necessarily every, provision.
A vote on a package does not isolate a view on each component.
